notes.front: What is Cloud Storage?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s object storage service: low-cost, highly durable object storage with no limit, for diverse data types.
notes.explanation: Data in it can be reached from anywhere, inside or outside Google Cloud, and optional redundancy across regions gives maximum reliability.
notes.example: Like a vast self-storage warehouse where every box has a unique label and can be fetched from anywhere in the world.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design an optimal storage strategy for your cloud workload”, “Object storage”
notes.evidence: Cloud Storage provides low-cost, highly durable, no-limit object storage for diverse data types. The data you store in Cloud Storage can be accessed from anywhere, within and outside Google Cloud. Optional redundancy across regions provides maximum reliability.

notes.front: What is a storage class in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A piece of metadata on every object that affects the object’s availability and pricing model.
notes.explanation: A bucket has a default storage class, which objects added to it inherit unless told otherwise.
notes.example: Like choosing between the front shelf, the back room and the off-site depot for stock, depending on how often you need it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Key concepts”
notes.evidence: A storage class is a piece of metadata that is used by every object. The storage class set for an object affects the object's availability and pricing model. When you create a bucket, you can specify a default storage class for the bucket. When you add objects to the bucket, they inherit this storage class unless explicitly set otherwise.

notes.front: What is a dual-region in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A bucket location that is a specific pair of regions, such as Tokyo and Osaka; the pair can be predefined or configurable.
notes.explanation: The location type you pick determines how the data is replicated and priced.
notes.example: Like keeping one copy of the family photos at home and another at a relative’s house in a named second city.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket locations”, “Key concepts”
notes.evidence: A dual-region is a specific pair of regions, such as Tokyo and Osaka (ASIA1). Dual-region pairings can be predefined or configurable. A multi-region is a large geographic area that contains two or more geographic regions, such as the United States (US). The location type determines how your data is replicated and priced.

notes.front: What is turbo replication in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A premium dual-region feature that gives a short, predictable recovery point objective.
notes.explanation: It speeds up replication between the two regions of a dual-region bucket.
notes.example: Like paying for a courier instead of second-class post, so the second copy arrives within a guaranteed time.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket locations”, “Location recommendations”
notes.evidence: If you need a short and predictable recovery point objective (RPO), enable the premium turbo replication feature.

notes.front: What is Object Lifecycle Management in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A feature that applies rules to objects, for example to delete them after a time, keep noncurrent versions, or move them to cheaper storage classes.
notes.explanation: It supports common needs such as a time to live for objects and “downgrading” storage classes to help manage costs.
notes.example: Like a filing policy that sends papers to the basement after a year and to the shredder after seven.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Lifecycle Management”, “Object Lifecycle Management”
notes.evidence: To support common use cases like setting a Time to Live (TTL) for objects, retaining noncurrent versions of objects, or "downgrading" storage classes of objects to help manage costs, Cloud Storage offers the Object Lifecycle Management feature.

notes.front: What is Autoclass in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A bucket feature that automatically moves each object to a suitable storage class based on its access pattern.
notes.explanation: Data that isn’t accessed moves to colder classes to cut storage cost, and data that is accessed moves to Standard storage.
notes.example: Like a librarian who moves books nobody borrows to the stacks, and brings a book back to the front shelf once someone asks for it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoclass”, “Autoclass”
notes.evidence: The Autoclass feature automatically transitions objects in your bucket to appropriate storage classes based on each object's access pattern. The feature moves data that isn't accessed to colder storage classes to reduce storage cost and moves data that is accessed to Standard storage to optimize future accesses.

notes.front: What is Object Versioning in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A bucket feature that keeps deleted or replaced objects as noncurrent versions, accessible until explicitly removed.
notes.explanation: It is used to track changes to objects and to recover specific versions of an object.
notes.example: Like a document editor’s version history, where every saved draft can be reopened.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Versioning”, “Object Versioning”
notes.evidence: Object Versioning preserves deleted objects as versioned, noncurrent objects that remain accessible in your bucket until explicitly removed. This feature is used to track changes to objects and to enable recovery of specific versions of an object.

notes.front: What is a retention policy on a Cloud Storage bucket?
notes.back: A bucket setting with a retention period: objects can be deleted or replaced only once their age exceeds that period.
notes.explanation: The policy applies to the objects already in the bucket as well as to new ones.
notes.example: Like a rule that invoices may not be shredded until they are six years old.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket Lock”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: You can add a retention policy to a bucket to specify a retention period. When a bucket retention policy is set, objects in the bucket can only be deleted or replaced once their age is greater than the retention period. The policy retroactively applies to existing objects in the bucket as well as new objects added to the bucket.

notes.front: What does Bucket Lock do to a bucket’s retention policy?
notes.back: It locks the policy permanently: once locked, it can’t be removed and its retention period can’t be reduced.
notes.explanation: Locking is irreversible, which is what makes the retention guarantee hold.
notes.example: Like sealing records in a time capsule that no key can open before the date on the lid.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket Lock”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: You can lock a bucket's retention policy to permanently set it on the bucket. Once you lock a policy, you cannot remove it or reduce the retention period it has.

notes.front: What is a signed URL in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A web address that carries a signature giving limited permission, for a limited time, to make a request on a resource.
notes.explanation: The authentication is in the query string, so users without credentials can perform specific actions.
notes.example: Like a day pass to a building: whoever holds it gets in, but only to one room and only until it expires.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Signed URLs”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: A signed URL is a URL that provides limited permission and time to make a request. Signed URLs contain authentication information, including a signature, in their query string, which allows users without credentials to perform specific actions on a resource.

notes.front: What is uniform bucket-level access in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A bucket setting that disables access control lists, so only bucket-level Identity and Access Management permissions grant access.
notes.explanation: Turning it on revokes all access that object access control lists had granted.
notes.example: Like replacing individual keys to every drawer with one keycard system at the office door.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Uniform bucket-level access”, “Uniform bucket-level access”
notes.evidence: When you enable uniform bucket-level access on a bucket, Access Control Lists (ACLs) are disabled, and only bucket-level Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions grant access to that bucket and the objects it contains. You revoke all access granted by object ACLs and the ability to administrate permissions using bucket ACLs.

notes.front: What is Hyperdisk?
notes.back: The fastest and most efficient durable disk for Compute Engine, recommended by Google for boot and data disks.
notes.explanation: It serves VMs, containers and bare metal instances alike.
notes.example: Like a network drive that behaves as if it were bolted inside the machine, and whose speed you can dial up or down.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google Cloud Hyperdisk overview”, “Google Cloud Hyperdisk overview”
notes.evidence: Hyperdisk is the fastest and most efficient durable disk for Compute Engine. If you need boot or data disks for your compute instances—virtual machine (VM) instances, containers, and bare metal instances—then Google recommends using Hyperdisk.

notes.front: What is Persistent Disk?
notes.back: One of Google Cloud’s two durable block storage offerings, alongside Hyperdisk, for data that must survive the VM stopping or failing.
notes.explanation: Persistent Disk isn’t available with the latest machine series.
notes.example: Like an external hard drive that stays safe on the desk even if the laptop is switched off or breaks.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Choose a disk type”, “Durable block storage”
notes.evidence: Durable, or persistent, block storage is for data that you want to preserve after you stop, suspend or delete the VM, or even if the VM crashes or fails. Hyperdisk and Persistent Disk are the durable block storage offerings in Google Cloud, but Persistent Disk isn't available with the latest machine series.

notes.front: What is a Hyperdisk Storage Pool?
notes.back: Hyperdisk capacity and performance bought in bulk, from which you create disks, instead of buying for each disk.
notes.explanation: Pooling simplifies planning, avoids overprovisioning storage and reduces costs.
notes.example: Like a family mobile plan with shared data, instead of a separate allowance for every phone.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google Cloud Hyperdisk overview”, “Hyperdisk features”
notes.evidence: Support for pooled capacity and performance: to simplify planning, avoid overprovisioning storage, and reduce costs, you can purchase Hyperdisk storage and performance in bulk by using Hyperdisk Storage Pools.

notes.front: What is Local SSD?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s temporary block storage: disks physically attached to the server that hosts your instance.
notes.explanation: It offers the fastest performance of all block storage types, but its data is lost if the VM stops for any reason.
notes.example: Like a whiteboard in the meeting room: quick to use, but wiped when the meeting ends.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Choose a disk type”, “Temporary block storage”
notes.evidence: Temporary, or ephemeral, block storage offers the fastest performance among all block storage types, with the tradeoff that the stored data is lost if the VM stops for any reason.

notes.front: What is a disk snapshot in Compute Engine?
notes.back: A backup that captures the contents of a disk at a specific point in time.
notes.explanation: There are three types, standard, instant and archive, and all capture a point-in-time copy.
notes.example: Like a photograph of a whiteboard before it is wiped: you can redraw the board exactly from it later.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About archive and standard disk snapshots”, “Snapshot types”
notes.evidence: You can back up a disk with snapshots. The three types of snapshots—standard, instant, and archive—all capture the contents of a disk at a specific point in time.

notes.front: What is Filestore?
notes.back: A fully managed file server on Google Cloud that clients such as Compute Engine VMs, GKE clusters and on-premises machines can connect to.
notes.explanation: Once provisioned, an instance’s capacity can be scaled as needed without downtime.
notes.example: Like the shared network drive in an office, but run for you in the cloud.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Filestore overview”, “Filestore overview”
notes.evidence: Filestore instances are fully managed file servers on Google Cloud that can be connected to a number of client types: Compute Engine VMs Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters External datastores such as Google Cloud VMware Engine On-premises machines Cloud Run services

notes.front: What is Google Cloud NetApp Volumes?
notes.back: A file storage service on Google Cloud that serves files over the network file protocols used by Linux and Windows, at a chosen service level.
notes.explanation: Its service levels are Flex, Standard, Premium and Extreme.
notes.example: Like a managed file share that both Linux and Windows desktops in an office can open.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design an optimal storage strategy for your cloud workload”, “File storage”
notes.evidence: NetApp Volumes File-based storage using NFS or SMB. You can choose a service level (Flex, Standard, Premium, or Extreme) that suits your use case.

notes.front: What are the three phases of Google’s design process for choosing storage for a cloud workload?
notes.back: Define the requirements, review the storage options, then select the services and features.
notes.explanation: Requirements come first: functional characteristics, security constraints, resilience, performance and cost goals.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design an optimal storage strategy for your cloud workload”, “Overview of the design process”
notes.evidence: you need to first consider the functional characteristics of the workload, security constraints, resilience requirements, performance expectations, and cost goals. Next, you need to review the available storage services and features in Google Cloud. Then, based on your requirements and the available options, you select the storage services and features that you need.

notes.front: Which storage format divides data into separately addressed chunks and is optimised for transaction processing?
notes.back: Block storage.
notes.explanation: Applications reach data by block address; it resembles an on-premises storage area network or directly attached storage.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design an optimal storage strategy for your cloud workload”, “Block storage”
notes.evidence: The data that you store in block storage is divided into chunks, each stored as a separate block with a unique address. Applications access data by referencing the appropriate block addresses. Block storage is optimized for high-IOPS workloads, such as transaction processing. It's similar to on-premises storage area network (SAN) and directly attached storage (DAS) systems.

notes.front: Which storage format organises data as a hierarchy of files in folders, reached by file name and directory path?
notes.back: File storage.
notes.explanation: It resembles on-premises network-attached storage, and clients mount the file system over a network protocol.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design an optimal storage strategy for your cloud workload”, “File storage”
notes.evidence: Data is organized and represented in a hierarchy of files that are stored in folders, similar to on-premises network-attached storage (NAS). File systems can be mounted on clients using protocols such as NFS and Server Message Block (SMB). Applications access data using the relevant filename and directory path.

notes.front: Which storage format keeps data as objects, each with a globally unique identifier, in a flat hierarchy of buckets?
notes.back: Object storage.
notes.explanation: Applications reach objects by their identifiers through web interfaces or client libraries, and metadata helps organise them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design an optimal storage strategy for your cloud workload”, “Object storage”
notes.evidence: Data is stored as objects in a flat hierarchy of buckets. Each object is assigned a globally unique ID. Objects can have system-assigned and user-defined metadata, to help you organize and manage the data. Applications access data by referencing the object IDs, using REST APIs or client libraries.

notes.front: Which Cloud Storage class is best for frequently accessed (“hot”) data and data kept only for brief periods?
notes.back: Standard storage.
notes.explanation: It is the class for hot data and for short-lived data alike.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Standard storage”
notes.evidence: Standard storage is best for data that is frequently accessed ("hot" data), as well as data that is stored for only brief periods of time.

notes.front: Which Cloud Storage class is ideal for data you read or modify on average once a month or less?
notes.back: Nearline storage.
notes.explanation: For data accessed less than once a quarter, Coldline or Archive are more cost-effective.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Nearline storage”
notes.evidence: Nearline storage is ideal for data you plan to read or modify on average once per month or less. For example, if you want to continuously add files to Cloud Storage and plan to access those files once a month for analysis, Nearline storage is a great choice.

notes.front: Which Cloud Storage class is ideal for data you read or modify at most once a quarter?
notes.back: Coldline storage.
notes.explanation: For data kept entirely for backup or archiving, Archive storage costs less still.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Coldline storage”
notes.evidence: Coldline storage is ideal for data you plan to read or modify at most once a quarter. Note, however, that for data being kept entirely for backup or archiving purposes, Archive storage is more cost-effective, as it offers the lowest storage costs.

notes.front: Which Cloud Storage class is the best choice for data you plan to access less than once a year?
notes.back: Archive storage.
notes.explanation: It is the lowest-cost class, meant for archiving, online backup and disaster recovery.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Archive storage”
notes.evidence: Archive storage is the lowest-cost, highly durable storage service for data archiving, online backup, and disaster recovery.

notes.front: Which newer Cloud Storage class stores data in zones beside your compute resources, for input/output-intensive workloads?
notes.back: Rapid storage, available only with zonal buckets through Rapid Bucket.
notes.explanation: Keeping objects in the same zone as compute gives much lower latency and higher throughput than other classes.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Rapid storage”
notes.evidence: Rapid storage is a high-performance storage class that's optimized for I/O-intensive workloads. When you use Rapid storage as a bucket's storage class, you can store your data in zonal locations. Storing your objects in the same zones as your compute resources enables significantly lower latency and higher throughput compared to other storage classes.

notes.front: Nearline storage has a minimum storage duration of {{c1::30 days}}.
notes.explanation: That minimum, slightly lower availability and data-access costs are the trade-offs for cheaper at-rest storage.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Nearline storage”
notes.evidence: Nearline storage is a better choice than Standard storage in scenarios where slightly lower availability, a 30-day minimum storage duration, and costs for data access are acceptable trade-offs for lowered at-rest storage costs.

notes.front: Coldline storage has a minimum storage duration of {{c1::90 days}}.
notes.explanation: In exchange for that minimum and higher access costs, it lowers at-rest storage costs further than Nearline.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Coldline storage”
notes.evidence: Coldline storage is a better choice than Standard storage or Nearline storage in scenarios where slightly lower availability, a 90-day minimum storage duration, and higher costs for data access are acceptable trade-offs for lowered at-rest storage costs.

notes.front: Archive storage has a minimum storage duration of {{c1::365 days}}.
notes.explanation: It also has higher costs for data access and operations than the other classes.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Archive storage”
notes.evidence: Archive storage also has higher costs for data access and operations, as well as a 365-day minimum storage duration.

notes.front: Which Cloud Storage classes charge retrieval fees?
notes.back: Nearline, Coldline and Archive storage.
notes.explanation: The same three are the classes with minimum storage durations: 30, 90 and 365 days.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Available storage classes”
notes.evidence: Nearline storage NEARLINE 30 days Yes 99.95% in multi-regions and dual-regions 99.9% in regions Coldline storage COLDLINE 90 days Yes 99.95% in multi-regions and dual-regions 99.9% in regions Archive storage ARCHIVE 365 days Yes

notes.front: How quickly can you read data kept in Archive storage?
notes.back: Within milliseconds, not hours or days.
notes.explanation: Unlike the “coldest” tiers of some other providers, Archive storage keeps data online.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Archive storage”
notes.evidence: Unlike the "coldest" storage services offered by other Cloud providers, your data is available within milliseconds, not hours or days.

notes.front: If you don’t specify a default storage class when you create a bucket, what does it get?
notes.back: Standard storage.
notes.explanation: Changing a bucket’s default later does not change the class of objects already in it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Key concepts”
notes.evidence: If you don't specify a default storage class when you create a bucket, that bucket's default storage class is set to Standard storage. Changing the default storage class of a bucket does not affect any of the objects that already exist in the bucket.

notes.front: What is a multi-region, as a Cloud Storage bucket location?
notes.back: A large geographic area containing two or more regions, such as the United States.
notes.explanation: It differs from a dual-region, which is a specific pair of regions.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket locations”, “Key concepts”
notes.evidence: A multi-region is a large geographic area that contains two or more geographic regions, such as the United States (US).

notes.front: What happens to a dual-region bucket’s availability if one of its regions fails?
notes.back: Failover and failback are automatic, with a recovery time objective of 0 and no need to change storage paths.
notes.explanation: Data is replicated across regions asynchronously, and the location has higher availability than a region.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket locations”, “Location considerations”
notes.evidence: Higher availability than regions for a given storage class Data redundancy across regions (asynchronous) Turbo replication option for replication within 15 minutes RTO(recovery time objective)=0: automated failover and failback on regional failure (no need to change storage paths)

notes.front: Which Cloud Storage location type has the lowest storage price and no replication charges?
notes.back: A region.
notes.explanation: Reading data within the same region also has no outbound data transfer charges; dual-regions and multi-regions charge for replication on write.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket locations”, “Location considerations”
notes.evidence: Lowest storage price No replication charges No outbound data transfer charges when reading data inside the same region Highest storage price Replication charges apply on write

notes.front: Turbo replication replicates a dual-region bucket’s data between its regions within {{c1::15 minutes}}.
notes.explanation: It is a premium dual-region feature, which Google advises turning on when you need a short and predictable recovery point objective.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket locations”, “Location considerations”
notes.evidence: Data redundancy across regions (asynchronous) Turbo replication option for replication within 15 minutes

notes.front: What does each Object Lifecycle Management rule contain, and when does its action run?
notes.back: One action and one or more conditions; the action runs only when an object matches all the conditions.
notes.explanation: A configuration is a set of such rules.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Lifecycle Management”, “Lifecycle configuration”
notes.evidence: Each lifecycle management configuration contains a set of rules. Each rule contains one action and one or more conditions. An object has to match all of the conditions specified in a rule for the action in the rule to be taken.

notes.front: Which lifecycle action removes an object once it meets the rule’s conditions?
notes.back: Delete.
notes.explanation: By default a deleted live object becomes soft-deleted and is kept for seven days, so it can still be restored.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Lifecycle Management”, “Delete”
notes.evidence: The Delete action deletes an object when the object meets all conditions specified in the lifecycle rule. By default, when you delete a live object, it becomes soft-deleted, and Cloud Storage retains it for a duration of seven days.

notes.front: Which lifecycle action moves an object to a different storage class?
notes.back: SetStorageClass.
notes.explanation: It also updates the object’s modification time; it can’t be used on buckets with Autoclass enabled.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Lifecycle Management”, “SetStorageClass”
notes.evidence: The SetStorageClass action changes the storage class of an object and updates the object's modification time when the object meets all conditions specified in the lifecycle rule.

notes.front: Which lifecycle action cleans up multipart uploads that never finished?
notes.back: AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload.
notes.explanation: It aborts the upload and deletes its parts, and only the age, matchesPrefix and matchesSuffix conditions can be used with it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Lifecycle Management”, “Abort incomplete multipart uploads”
notes.evidence: The AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action aborts an incomplete multipart upload and deletes the associated parts when the multipart upload meets the conditions specified in the lifecycle rule. Only the following lifecycle conditions can be used with this action: age matchesPrefix matchesSuffix

notes.front: If a Delete rule and a SetStorageClass rule both match an object at the same time, which action happens?
notes.back: Delete.
notes.explanation: Cloud Storage performs only one action; Delete takes precedence over any SetStorageClass.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Lifecycle Management”, “Lifecycle configuration”
notes.evidence: If multiple rules have their conditions satisfied simultaneously for a single object, Cloud Storage performs the action associated with only one of the rules, based on the following considerations: The Delete action takes precedence over any SetStorageClass action.

notes.front: Can an application count on a lifecycle action happening as soon as an object meets the rule’s conditions?
notes.back: No. Actions run asynchronously, so there can be a lag before the action is taken.
notes.explanation: An object due for deletion may stay visible for a while until the action is executed.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Lifecycle Management”, “Lifecycle behavior”
notes.evidence: Cloud Storage performs an action asynchronously, so there can be a lag between when the conditions are satisfied and when the action is taken. Your applications shouldn't rely on lifecycle actions occurring within a certain amount of time after a lifecycle condition is met.

notes.front: The lifecycle age condition is measured from the object’s {{c1::creation time}}.
notes.explanation: An object’s age is unaffected by it becoming a noncurrent version.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Lifecycle Management”, “Age”
notes.evidence: The age condition is satisfied when a resource reaches the specified age (in days). Age is measured from the resource's creation time.

notes.front: Under Autoclass, which class does a new object start in, and where does it end up by default if never accessed?
notes.back: It starts in Standard storage and, by default, ends in Nearline storage until it is accessed.
notes.explanation: You can optionally make Archive storage the terminal class instead.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoclass”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: Most objects transition to progressively colder storage classes if they're not accessed. By default, the terminal storage class for Autoclass is Nearline storage, which means objects transition to Nearline storage and remain in that storage class until they're accessed. Optionally, you can configure Autoclass so that the terminal storage class is Archive storage.

notes.front: Under Autoclass, an object that isn’t accessed for {{c1::30 days}} transitions to Nearline storage.
notes.explanation: If the object’s data is accessed, it moves back to Standard storage.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoclass”, “Autoclass transitions”
notes.evidence: If an object's data is accessed, the object transitions to Standard storage. Any object that isn't accessed for 30 days transitions to Nearline storage.

notes.front: Under Autoclass, objects smaller than {{c1::128 KiB}} never move to colder storage classes.
notes.explanation: They stay in Standard storage permanently; only object data, not metadata, counts towards the size.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoclass”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: Objects smaller than 128 KiB don't transition to colder storage classes. Instead, they are permanently stored in Standard storage. Only object data, not object metadata, is considered when determining whether the object is smaller than 128 KiB.

notes.front: When is Autoclass not recommended for a bucket?
notes.back: When most of the bucket’s data clearly fits the use cases of particular storage classes.
notes.explanation: It suits data with varied or unknown access patterns, not data whose pattern you already know.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoclass”, “Should you use Autoclass?”
notes.evidence: However, Autoclass isn't recommended if the majority of your bucket's data fits into the use cases of specific storage classes.

notes.front: What does Google recommend instead of Object Versioning to protect against permanent loss from accidental or malicious deletion?
notes.back: Soft delete.
notes.explanation: Object Versioning does not protect against a bucket being deleted; objects can be recovered from a deleted bucket only with soft delete.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Versioning”, “Object Versioning”
notes.evidence: We recommend that you use soft delete instead of Object Versioning to protect against permanent data loss from accidental or malicious deletions. To learn more about when to use soft delete and Object Versioning, see Considerations. Caution: Objects can only be recovered from a deleted bucket when soft delete is enabled. Object Versioning does not provide protection against bucket deletions.

notes.front: Once a bucket’s retention policy is locked, what can you still change about it?
notes.back: You can increase the retention period. You can never reduce it or remove the policy.
notes.explanation: Trying to remove or shorten a locked policy fails with an error.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket Lock”, “Retention policy locks”
notes.evidence: When you lock a bucket's retention policy, you prevent the policy from ever being removed or the retention period from ever being reduced (although you can still increase the retention period).

notes.front: When can you delete a bucket whose retention policy is locked?
notes.back: Only when every object in it has met the retention period.
notes.explanation: Locking a retention policy is irreversible, so the policy protects the bucket itself as well as each object in it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket Lock”, “Retention policy locks”
notes.evidence: Once a retention policy is locked, you cannot delete the bucket until every object in the bucket has met the retention period.

notes.front: Under a retention policy, what happens to the age of an object when you replace it?
notes.back: The new version’s age restarts at zero.
notes.explanation: The retention period then runs again from the replacement.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket Lock”, “Bucket retention policies”
notes.evidence: If you decided to replace Object B, this new version of Object B has an age that restarts at 0 years.

notes.front: Who can use an active signed URL?
notes.back: Anyone who has it, whether or not they have a valid account.
notes.explanation: The signature, not the user’s identity, grants the time-limited access.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Signed URLs”, “Signed URLs”
notes.evidence: This page provides an overview of signed URLs, which use signatures to give time-limited access to a specific Cloud Storage resource. Anyone in possession of the signed URL can use it while it's active, regardless of whether they have a valid account.

notes.front: What ends a signed URL’s access?
notes.back: Reaching its expiration time, or rotating the key used to sign it.
notes.explanation: You set the expiration time when you create the signed URL.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Signed URLs”, “Should you use a signed URL?”
notes.evidence: You specify an expiration time when you create the signed URL. Anyone who knows the URL can access the resource until the expiration time for the URL is reached or the key used to sign the URL is rotated.

notes.front: Uniform bucket-level access can’t be disabled after it has been active on a bucket for {{c1::90}} consecutive days.
notes.explanation: After that point, access through Identity and Access Management alone is permanent for the bucket.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Uniform bucket-level access”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: Uniform bucket-level access cannot be disabled after it has been active on a bucket for 90

notes.front: Why is uniform bucket-level access generally recommended?
notes.back: It unifies and simplifies how access is granted and prevents unintended data exposure from access control lists.
notes.explanation: Some features, such as managed folders and hierarchical namespace, also require it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Uniform bucket-level access”, “Should you use uniform bucket-level access?”
notes.evidence: Generally, using uniform bucket-level access is recommended: Uniform bucket-level access unifies and simplifies how you grant access to your Cloud Storage resources. Uniform bucket-level access prevents unintended data exposure from ACLs.

notes.front: Between Hyperdisk and Persistent Disk, which does Google recommend, and why?
notes.back: Hyperdisk, for the highest performance and advanced features.
notes.explanation: Persistent Disk isn’t available with the latest machine series.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Choose a disk type”, “Durable block storage”
notes.evidence: Hyperdisk and Persistent Disk are the durable block storage offerings in Google Cloud, but Persistent Disk isn't available with the latest machine series. Google recommends using Hyperdisk for the highest performance and advanced features.

notes.front: Can the data on a Hyperdisk or Persistent Disk volume outlive the VM it is attached to?
notes.back: Yes. Volumes are independent of instances, so you can detach one and keep the data after deleting the instance.
notes.explanation: For the same reason, you can attach a volume to a running instance without downtime.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Choose a disk type”, “Durable block storage”
notes.evidence: Portability: Hyperdisk and Persistent Disk volumes are independent of the compute instances that you attach them to. This characteristic means you can attach a volume to a running instance without downtime. You can also detach the volume to keep your data even after you delete the instance.

notes.front: Which Hyperdisk type do you need to replicate a disk’s data to another zone in the same region?
notes.back: Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability, the only Hyperdisk type supported for zonal replication.
notes.explanation: Its data is replicated synchronously across two zones, protecting against up to one zonal outage.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google Cloud Hyperdisk overview”, “Synchronous replication”
notes.evidence: To replicate data to another zone within the same region, you must use Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes. Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability is the only supported Hyperdisk type for zonal replication.

notes.front: How can you protect a Hyperdisk volume’s data against a regional outage?
notes.back: Enable Asynchronous Replication, which keeps a copy of the volume in another region.
notes.explanation: If the primary region becomes unavailable, you can use the secondary volume.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google Cloud Hyperdisk overview”, “Cross-regional asynchronous replication”
notes.evidence: You can protect your data in the unlikely event of a regional outage by enabling Asynchronous Replication. Asynchronous Replication maintains a copy of the data on your volume in another region.

notes.front: When is data on Local SSD lost?
notes.back: Whenever the VM stops, is suspended or restarts, or crashes or fails.
notes.explanation: Being ephemeral, it should hold only scratch data, caches or data for flash-optimised databases, and it can’t be a boot volume.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Choose a disk type”, “Temporary block storage”
notes.evidence: Data is lost if you stop, suspend, or restart the VM, or if the VM crashes or fails. Because of its ephemeral nature, use temporary block storage for only scratch data, caches such as tempdb for Microsoft SQL Server, or storage for flash-optimized databases. You can't use temporary block storage as a boot volume.

notes.front: After a disk’s first full snapshot, what does its second snapshot contain?
notes.back: Only data that is new or changed since the first, plus references to the first for unchanged data.
notes.explanation: Every later snapshot works the same way, always based on the last successful snapshot.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About archive and standard disk snapshots”, “How incremental snapshots work”
notes.evidence: The first successful snapshot of a disk is a full snapshot that contains all the data on the disk. The second snapshot only contains any new data or modified data since the first snapshot. Data that hasn't changed since Snapshot 1 isn't included. Instead, Snapshot 2 contains references to Snapshot 1 for any unchanged data.

notes.front: Which snapshot type is deleted when its source disk is deleted?
notes.back: An instant snapshot. Standard and archive snapshots survive the disk’s deletion.
notes.explanation: To keep a backup after deleting a disk, use a standard or archive snapshot.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About archive and standard disk snapshots”, “Retention after source disk deletion”
notes.evidence: An instant snapshot of a disk only exists until the source disk is deleted. Standard and archive snapshots aren't deleted with the source disk. Therefore, if you want to retain a backup of a disk after you delete the disk itself, use archive or standard snapshots.

notes.front: Which snapshot type gives the fastest recovery, and which the slowest?
notes.back: Instant snapshots are fastest and archive snapshots slowest, with standard snapshots in between.
notes.explanation: Archive snapshots are the slowest to restore but offer the most cost-efficient storage.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About archive and standard disk snapshots”, “Data recovery time”
notes.evidence: Instant snapshots offer the lowest and best recovery times. Standard snapshots have faster data recovery times than archive snapshots. Archive snapshots have the longest data recovery times, but offer the most cost efficient storage.

notes.front: Which snapshot storage location should you choose to meet a data-placement policy?
notes.back: The nearest regional location that complies with the policy.
notes.explanation: A regional location gives more control over where data sits; a multi-regional one gives the highest availability.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About archive and standard disk snapshots”, “Snapshot storage location types”
notes.evidence: A multi-regional storage location provides the highest availability and resilience. A regional storage location gives you more control over the physical location of your data because you specify a single region. If you need to comply with corporate or government data-placement policies, store your snapshot in the nearest regional location that complies with these policies.

notes.front: What does Filestore give GKE users that block storage such as Persistent Disk offers only in limited form?
notes.back: Multiple-reader, multiple-writer access: volumes mounted read-write by many nodes at once.
notes.explanation: Filestore supports many application instances using the same file system simultaneously.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Filestore overview”, “Why Filestore?”
notes.evidence: For Google Kubernetes Engine users, for example, Filestore provides multiple reader, multiple writer access, letting you mount your GKE PersistentVolumes as read-write by many nodes. Filestore offers a versatile alternative to block storage products, such as Persistent Disk, which support only limited options for multiple writer access to a disk.

notes.front: An architect is asked to pick storage for a new analytics workload. A colleague suggests starting by comparing Filestore and Cloud Storage prices. What should come first?
notes.back: D: define the workload’s requirements first.
notes.choices:
A) Pick the cheapest service, then adapt the workload
B) Review every storage service’s features
C) Choose Hyperdisk as the recommended default
D) Define the workload’s requirements: function, security, resilience, performance and cost
notes.choicesExplained: A reverses the process and may fail requirements. B is the second phase, which needs requirements to judge options against. C picks a product before knowing whether block storage fits at all.
notes.explanation: The design process starts with requirements, then reviews options, then selects.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design an optimal storage strategy for your cloud workload”, “Overview of the design process”
notes.evidence: As a cloud architect, when you plan storage for a cloud workload, you need to first consider the functional characteristics of the workload, security constraints, resilience requirements, performance expectations, and cost goals.

notes.front: Twenty VMs running a rendering app must read and write the same file system at the same time, with file locking. Which service fits?
notes.back: A: Filestore.
notes.choices:
A) Filestore
B) One Persistent Disk attached to every VM
C) Local SSD on each VM
D) A Cloud Storage bucket used as a disk
notes.choicesExplained: B: block storage offers only limited options for multiple writers. C is separate, temporary storage on each VM, not a shared file system. D is object storage; tools that mount it lack capabilities such as file locking.
notes.explanation: As file storage, Filestore lets many application instances use the same file system simultaneously.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Filestore overview”, “Why Filestore?”
notes.evidence: As a type of persistent file storage, Filestore supports multiple concurrent application instances accessing the same file system simultaneously.

notes.front: A team adds files to Cloud Storage continuously and reads them once a month for a report. Which storage class keeps costs lowest?
notes.back: C: Nearline storage.
notes.choices:
A) Standard storage
B) Archive storage
C) Nearline storage
D) Rapid storage
notes.choicesExplained: A costs more at rest for data read only monthly. B suits data read less than once a year; monthly reads would bring high access costs. D is a high-performance zonal class for input/output-intensive work.
notes.explanation: Nearline suits data read or modified about once a month or less.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Nearline storage”
notes.evidence: Nearline storage is ideal for data you plan to read or modify on average once per month or less. For example, if you want to continuously add files to Cloud Storage and plan to access those files once a month for analysis, Nearline storage is a great choice.

notes.front: To save money, a team writes daily temporary files to Coldline storage and deletes each file after two weeks. Why is this a poor choice?
notes.back: D: Coldline has a 90-day minimum storage duration.
notes.choices:
A) Coldline can’t hold files smaller than a set size
B) Coldline data is offline and takes hours to read
C) Coldline can’t be used in a region
D) Coldline has a 90-day minimum storage duration, a trade-off meant for data kept far longer than two weeks
notes.choicesExplained: A: there is no minimum object size in any class. B: Cloud Storage offers low latency with no offline retrieval. C: Coldline is available in regions.
notes.explanation: Short-lived data suits Standard storage, which has no minimum duration.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Coldline storage”
notes.evidence: Coldline storage is a better choice than Standard storage or Nearline storage in scenarios where slightly lower availability, a 90-day minimum storage duration, and higher costs for data access are acceptable trade-offs for lowered at-rest storage costs.

notes.front: A website’s product images are read thousands of times a day. Someone proposes moving them from Standard to Archive storage to cut the bill. What is the main problem?
notes.back: C: every read would add retrieval fees, on top of higher access costs.
notes.choices:
A) Archive storage is offline
B) Archive storage is less durable
C) Every read would add retrieval fees, and Archive has higher access costs
D) Archive storage can’t serve objects over the internet
notes.choicesExplained: A: Archive data is available within milliseconds. B: all classes share the same high durability. D: all classes are accessible worldwide.
notes.explanation: Retrieval fees apply to Nearline, Coldline and Archive, which suit rarely read data.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Storage classes”, “Available storage classes”
notes.evidence: Nearline storage NEARLINE 30 days Yes 99.95% in multi-regions and dual-regions 99.9% in regions Coldline storage COLDLINE 90 days Yes 99.95% in multi-regions and dual-regions 99.9% in regions Archive storage ARCHIVE 365 days Yes

notes.front: A company needs its bucket data in two specific regions for disaster recovery, and wants a short, predictable recovery point objective. Which location setup fits?
notes.back: B: a dual-region with turbo replication.
notes.choices:
A) A single region
B) A dual-region with turbo replication
C) A zonal bucket
D) A multi-region
notes.choicesExplained: A keeps data in one region. D spans regions but doesn’t give precise control over where the copies are. C is limited to one zone.
notes.explanation: Dual-regions give cross-region redundancy with precise control of locations, and turbo replication gives a short, predictable recovery point.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket locations”, “Location recommendations”
notes.evidence: Cross-region redundancy, with precise control of the locations where copies of data are stored Dual-region3 Analytics Backup and archive Disaster recovery

notes.front: Application logs land in Standard storage. They should move to Coldline after 30 days and be deleted after a year, with no manual work. What should the team configure?
notes.back: A: Object Lifecycle Management rules with SetStorageClass and Delete actions.
notes.choices:
A) Object Lifecycle Management rules with SetStorageClass and Delete actions
B) A locked retention policy of one year
C) Object Versioning
D) Signed URLs that expire after a year
notes.choicesExplained: B stops deletion before a year but never deletes or moves anything. C keeps more copies, not fewer. D controls access, not storage class or deletion.
notes.explanation: Lifecycle rules can “downgrade” storage classes and set a time to live for objects.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Lifecycle Management”, “Object Lifecycle Management”
notes.evidence: To support common use cases like setting a Time to Live (TTL) for objects, retaining noncurrent versions of objects, or "downgrading" storage classes of objects to help manage costs, Cloud Storage offers the Object Lifecycle Management feature.

notes.front: A media library’s access patterns are unpredictable: some files are popular for a week, others are never opened again. Which Cloud Storage option manages classes with least effort?
notes.back: D: Autoclass.
notes.choices:
A) Coldline storage for everything
B) Object Versioning
C) Lifecycle rules keyed on object age
D) Autoclass
notes.choicesExplained: A penalises the popular files with access costs. C moves objects by age, not by whether they are read. B keeps versions; it does not change classes.
notes.explanation: Google recommends Autoclass when access frequency varies or the retention period is unknown.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design an optimal storage strategy for your cloud workload”, “Storage recommendations”
notes.evidence: Access frequency varies, or the data-retention period is unknown or not predictable. Use the Autoclass feature to automatically transition objects in a bucket to appropriate storage classes based on each object's access pattern.

notes.front: A team keeps configuration files in a bucket and wants to recover an earlier version after someone overwrites a file by mistake. Which feature keeps those older versions?
notes.back: D: Object Versioning.
notes.choices:
A) Uniform bucket-level access
B) Autoclass
C) Turbo replication
D) Object Versioning
notes.choicesExplained: A controls who can access the bucket. B changes storage classes. C speeds up replication of the current data, overwrites included.
notes.explanation: With versioning enabled, each replacement or deletion keeps a noncurrent version identified by its generation number.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Object Versioning”, “Introduction”
notes.evidence: Cloud Storage retains a noncurrent object version each time you replace or delete a live object version, as long as you don't specify the generation number of the live version.

notes.front: Regulations say trading records must be kept for seven years, and no one, including administrators, may shorten that period later. What should the bucket use?
notes.back: C: a seven-year retention policy, locked with Bucket Lock.
notes.choices:
A) A lifecycle rule to delete objects after seven years
B) An unlocked seven-year retention policy
C) A seven-year retention policy, locked with Bucket Lock
D) Archive storage
notes.choicesExplained: B can be removed or reduced by someone with permission. A deletes after seven years but doesn’t stop earlier deletion. D lowers cost but protects nothing.
notes.explanation: A locked policy can’t be removed or reduced, and it applies to existing and new objects.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Bucket Lock”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: You can lock a bucket's retention policy to permanently set it on the bucket. Once you lock a policy, you cannot remove it or reduce the retention period it has.

notes.front: A web app lets customers without Google accounts upload a photo straight to Cloud Storage. Access should last only a few minutes and be decided by the app’s own logic. What should the app hand out?
notes.back: B: a signed URL with a short expiration time.
notes.choices:
A) Public write access to the bucket
B) A signed URL with a short expiration time
C) Uniform bucket-level access
D) Identity and Access Management roles for each customer
notes.choicesExplained: A lets anyone write at any time. D needs each customer to have an account. C governs how permissions are granted but gives the customers nothing.
notes.explanation: Signed URLs give time-limited read, write or delete access to users without their own accounts.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Signed URLs”, “Should you use a signed URL?”
notes.evidence: you might not want to require your users to have their own account in order to access Cloud Storage, but you still want to control access using your application-specific logic. The typical way to address this use case is to provide a signed URL to a user

notes.front: An audit finds objects exposed through old per-object access control lists. The security team wants access granted only through Identity and Access Management at bucket level. What should it enable?
notes.back: B: uniform bucket-level access.
notes.choices:
A) Object Versioning
B) Uniform bucket-level access
C) A retention policy
D) Signed URLs
notes.choicesExplained: A keeps old object versions. C stops deletion, not access. D adds a way in rather than closing one.
notes.explanation: It disables access control lists and prevents unintended data exposure from them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Uniform bucket-level access”, “Should you use uniform bucket-level access?”
notes.evidence: Uniform bucket-level access unifies and simplifies how you grant access to your Cloud Storage resources. Uniform bucket-level access prevents unintended data exposure from ACLs.

notes.front: A database needs much more disk performance, but its data size isn’t growing. The team doesn’t want to pay for capacity it won’t use. Which disk choice fits?
notes.back: D: Hyperdisk, raising performance without changing size.
notes.choices:
A) A bigger Persistent Disk
B) Local SSD as the main database disk
C) A snapshot schedule
D) Hyperdisk, raising performance without changing size
notes.choicesExplained: A buys capacity to get speed: Persistent Disk performance depends on size. B loses the data if the VM stops. C is a backup, not performance.
notes.explanation: Hyperdisk performance is independent of provisioned capacity.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Choose a disk type”, “Differences between Hyperdisk and Persistent Disk”
notes.evidence: Hyperdisk performance is independent of provisioned capacity. This feature means that you can increase or decrease a Hyperdisk volume's performance without changing its size. Unlike Hyperdisk, Persistent Disk performance depends on provisioned capacity. Consequently, to improve a Persistent Disk volume's performance, you must increase its size.

notes.front: A video transcoder needs the fastest possible scratch space for intermediate files it can regenerate. Losing them if the VM restarts is acceptable. What should it use?
notes.back: A: Local SSD.
notes.choices:
A) Local SSD
B) Filestore
C) Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability
D) Nearline storage
notes.choicesExplained: B is shared file storage, not the fastest local scratch. C adds zonal replication the throwaway data doesn’t need. D is object storage for rarely read data.
notes.explanation: Google recommends Local SSD for a fast scratch disk or cache.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design an optimal storage strategy for your cloud workload”, “Storage recommendations”
notes.evidence: Requirement Recommendation Fast scratch disk or cache Use local SSD disks (ephemeral).

notes.front: For compliance, a firm must keep disk backups for seven years and expects almost never to restore them. Which snapshot type is the best fit?
notes.back: C: archive snapshots.
notes.choices:
A) Instant snapshots
B) Standard snapshots
C) Archive snapshots
D) A Local SSD copy
notes.choicesExplained: A disappears if the source disk is deleted. B works but costs more for long retention. D is temporary storage lost when the VM stops.
notes.explanation: Archive snapshots are lower-cost and suited to compliance, audit and long-term cold storage.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About archive and standard disk snapshots”, “Archive snapshots”
notes.evidence: However, archive snapshots are lower-cost and are better suited for use cases related to compliance, audit, and long-term cold storage. If you require snapshot retention for many months or years and rarely need to access snapshots, consider using archive snapshots instead of standard snapshots.

notes.front: A 2-terabyte disk is snapshotted every night, and about 10 gigabytes change each day. Roughly how much new data does each night’s snapshot hold after the first?
notes.back: B: about 10 gigabytes of changed data.
notes.choices:
A) The full 2 terabytes
B) About 10 gigabytes of changed data
C) Nothing: snapshots only store references
D) 1 terabyte, half the disk
notes.choicesExplained: A describes only the first, full snapshot. C: later snapshots hold new and changed data as well as references. D has no basis.
notes.explanation: A snapshot’s size shows how much data changed since the previous snapshot.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “About archive and standard disk snapshots”, “Snapshot size”
notes.evidence: A standard or archive snapshot's size shows how much data has changed on the source disk since the previous snapshot was created.

notes.front: A company is moving Windows file shares that clients reach over the Server Message Block protocol. Which Google Cloud file service does Google recommend?
notes.back: D: Google Cloud NetApp Volumes.
notes.choices:
A) Filestore
B) Cloud Storage
C) Persistent Disk
D) Google Cloud NetApp Volumes
notes.choicesExplained: A serves the Network File System protocol (versions 3 and 4.1), not Server Message Block. B is object storage. C is block storage for a VM.
notes.explanation: For that protocol, the recommendation is simply to use NetApp Volumes.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Design an optimal storage strategy for your cloud workload”, “Storage recommendations”
notes.evidence: SMB Use NetApp Volumes.

notes.front: A database’s data disk must survive the loss of one zone without restoring from backup. Which option fits?
notes.back: A: Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability.
notes.choices:
A) Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability
B) Local SSD
C) A daily archive snapshot
D) A Hyperdisk Storage Pool
notes.choicesExplained: B is lost when the VM stops. C means restoring from backup and losing recent writes. D pools capacity and performance but doesn’t replicate across zones.
notes.explanation: Its data is replicated synchronously across two zones in a region, protecting against up to one zonal outage.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google Cloud Hyperdisk overview”, “Hyperdisk features”
notes.evidence: To protect your data in case of a zonal outage, use Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability. Data on Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes is synchronously replicated across two zones within the same region to protect against up to one zonal outage.

notes.front: How does raising performance differ between Hyperdisk and Persistent Disk?
notes.back: Hyperdisk performance is set independently of size; Persistent Disk performance depends on capacity, so you must enlarge the disk.
notes.explanation: Hyperdisk also has higher limits for operations per second and throughput.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Choose a disk type”, “Differences between Hyperdisk and Persistent Disk”
notes.evidence: Unlike Hyperdisk, Persistent Disk performance depends on provisioned capacity. Consequently, to improve a Persistent Disk volume's performance, you must increase its size. Better overall performance: Hyperdisk has higher IOPS and throughput limits than Persistent Disk.

notes.front: How do Filestore’s zonal and regional tiers differ in purpose?
notes.back: Zonal: high throughput and low latency for localised work such as batch or rendering. Regional: continuous availability and regional resilience for mission-critical workloads.
notes.explanation: The tiers vary in capacity, performance and features, each tailored to particular uses.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Filestore overview”, “Service tiers”
notes.evidence: Zonal tier: Optimized for HPC, batch compute, media rendering, and localized workloads requiring high throughput and low latency. Regional tier: Designed for mission-critical workloads requiring continuous availability and regional resilience.
